summary: This unit teaches you to plan, write, check and issue the basic technical reports used in a welding and fabrication business: inspection and test reports, condition surveys, incident reports, non-conformance reports, progress reports and recommendation reports. You will learn to agree terms of reference, gather accurate evidence, present data in tables and charts, write findings, conclusions and recommendations that a reader can act on, and see a report through checking, approval, issue and filing.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 3 you do more than fill in forms: you decide what a report must cover, gather the evidence, write it so that the reader can act on it, check other people's reports, and see each report through approval, issue and filing.

A **technical report** is a written record of facts about a job, a test, a failure or a piece of equipment, set out so that someone else can understand them and decide what to do. In a fabrication shop, reports protect people (a cracked handrail weld must be dealt with), protect the business (the client can see the work was inspected), and help the team improve (a reject figure that keeps rising shows where to look).

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders who lead a team, inspect work or deal with clients. The examples come from welding and fabrication, but the same skills serve any trade.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Agree what the report is for
Find out who will read it, what question it must answer, what it must cover and by when: the terms of reference.
Plan the report and gather evidence
Decide what data is needed, measure and record it accurately with units, number every item, and take photos with a scale and a label.
Choose the right kind of report
Inspection, test, condition survey, incident, non-conformance, progress, recommendation or completion report, or a short memo or form.
Organise the report
Use a clear structure: title page, summary, introduction, method, findings, discussion, conclusions, recommendations, references and appendices.
Present data clearly
Put readings in numbered tables, choose the right chart, label the axes with units, and show the numbers behind every percentage.
Write clearly and objectively
Plain words, short sentences, the active voice, one term for one thing; facts kept apart from opinions; nothing left out because it is unwelcome.
Draw conclusions and make recommendations
Say what the findings mean, find the cause, and give specific actions with who and when, in order of priority.
Check, approve, issue and file
Check figures against the records, have the report checked and approved, issue it with a number, correct it only by a new issue, send it to the distribution list and keep it as long as required.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on kinds of report, terms of reference, structure, tables and graphs, accuracy, clear language, objectivity, and checking, issue and filing.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as glossary, caption, disposition and distribution list) and essays in which you explain how to plan, write and issue a report.

Two **group practicals**: inspecting a set of welded samples and writing a weld inspection report with a table and a bar chart; and surveying steel items at the Centre, writing a recommendation report with priorities, and presenting it.

blocks.note: In the practicals the assessor watches how you work as well as what you hand in: whether you record readings with units, label your photos, check another member's section, and make your recommendations follow from your findings.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Reports at work and the kinds of report

blocks.p: Every report answers a question for a reader. The kind of report depends on that question.

head: Kind of report
The question it answers
Typical contents
rows: Inspection report
Does this work meet the drawing and the specification?
Items inspected, method and gauges used, readings, defects against the acceptance limits, accept or reject for each item
Test report
What were the results of this test, and did they pass?
The test procedure or standard, each specimen and its identification, the equipment, results with the acceptance limit beside each, pass or fail
Condition survey report
What state is this existing structure or item in?
Each defect with its location, size, photo number and how serious it is; what could not be inspected
Incident investigation report
What happened, why, and how do we stop it happening again?
Date, time, place, people, the sequence of events, injury or damage, immediate and root causes, corrective actions with names and dates
Non-conformance report (NCR)
What does not meet the requirement, and what will be done about it?
The requirement, what was found, the items affected, the cause, the disposition, the corrective action and the close-out
Progress report
Is the job on time and on budget?
Planned against actual progress, problems and their causes, the effect on the finish date and cost, recovery actions, decisions needed
Recommendation report
Which option should we choose, or what should we do?
The options, how they were compared (cost, safety, quality, time), the findings and one clear recommendation
Job completion report
Is the job finished, and is anything still open?
What was done, the checks and their results, problems met, outstanding items, client sign-off

blocks.p: A report does not have to be long. A **form** (such as an inspection record or an NCR form) suits routine reports, because the same facts are needed every time. A **memo or email report** of a page suits a short matter for one reader. A **full report** with sections suits a bigger question, several readers, or a report that may be used as evidence later.

blocks.note: The kind of report decides the content, not the length. A one-page NCR can matter more than a 12-page progress report, because it stops faulty work going out.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Why reports matter in welding and fabrication

ul: **Safety:** a defect in a handrail, a lifting lug or a tank stand can hurt someone. A report makes sure it is dealt with.
**Quality and the contract:** clients and engineers want proof that the work was inspected against the specification.
**Traceability:** records link each weld to its welder, its materials, its procedure and its inspection, so a problem found later can be traced.
**Evidence:** insurers, government safety inspectors and courts may read incident and inspection reports long after the event.
**Improvement:** figures collected over months show trends: which defect keeps coming back, which kind of job always runs late.

sections.title: Planning the report: purpose, reader and terms of reference

blocks.p: Most weak reports go wrong before the first word is written: the writer was not clear what the report was for or who would read it. Plan first.
The **terms of reference** set out what the report must cover, for whom, and by when. Agree them with the person who asked for the report, and write them in the introduction. They usually include:

ul: **Purpose:** the question the report must answer, for example 'Are the welds on the 12 loading-ramp frames fit for use?'
**Scope:** what is included and what is not, for example 'the welded joints only, not the paintwork or the bolts'.
**Reader:** who asked for it, and who else will read it.
**Deadline and form:** when it is needed, and how (printed, PDF, on the company's form).
**Limits:** anything that restricts the work, such as access, time or weather, for example 'inspected from the ground only'.

blocks.note: If the person asking cannot say what question the report must answer, ask: 'What will you decide when you read it?' The answer is the purpose.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The facts stay the same for every reader, but the order, the detail and the words change.

head: Reader
What they want
How to write for them
rows: Client or member of the public
Is it safe? What will you do, when, and what will it cost?
Plain words, trade terms explained, a short letter or summary, a named contact
Works manager or supervisor
The answer, the cost, the risk and the decision needed, quickly
Summary first, then the detail; recommendations that say who and when
Welding team
Exactly what went wrong and what to change
Specific technical facts, photos or sketches, the new method; often a briefing as well as a note
Engineer or inspector
The evidence and how it was gathered
The full method, readings with units, the standard and its limits, instrument numbers, traceable records

blocks.p: A busy manager may read only the **summary** and the **recommendations**. Make sure those two parts can stand on their own.

flow: Agree the terms of reference: purpose, scope, reader, deadline
Decide what data you need to answer the question, and how you will get it
Prepare: record sheets, gauges and tapes in date, a camera, markers, the drawing and the specification with its limits
Gather the evidence and record it at the time, with units, locations and photo numbers
Sort and check the data; work out totals, averages and percentages
Outline the report: the headings first, then the main point of each section
Write the draft, check it, and have it checked and approved
Issue it to the distribution list and file it

blocks.note: Decide the question and the data you need **before** you collect anything. Data gathered without a question is usually the wrong data, or far too much of it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A report is only as good as the evidence behind it. Record facts when you find them, not from memory later.

head: Kind
What it is
Examples
rows: Quantitative
Measured or counted numbers
Leg lengths, undercut depths, the number of rejects, hours worked, temperatures
Qualitative
Descriptions and observations
'Heavy rust at the base of post 3', 'paint flaking', a witness's account
Primary
Data you collect yourself for this report
Your own measurements, photos and interviews
Secondary
Data that already exists
Drawings, the welding procedure specification (WPS), mill certificates, earlier reports, the maker's data

ul: Write every reading **with its unit**: 6.5 mm, not 6.5.

Record to the **resolution of the instrument**: a gauge that reads in 0.5 mm steps gives 6.5 mm, not 6.48 mm; a caliper that reads to 0.01 mm gives 12.37 mm. Do not add figures the instrument cannot show, and do not round off figures it can.
Note which instrument you used (its number), and check that it is in calibration.

Write in ink on the record sheet at the time. If you make a mistake, cross it out with one line so it can still be read, write the correct figure beside it and initial it. Never rub out or write over a reading.
Note the conditions if they matter: the date, the time, the temperature, rain or wind.

blocks.p: **Traceability** is the ability to link a finished part back to its materials, its welder, its procedure and its inspection records. Number every item before you inspect it.

ul: Give each item and each weld a number, marked on the job with a paint marker or a label, and shown on a sketch or **weld map**.
Record each welder's identification (name, number or stamp) against the welds he or she made.
Record the material's heat or batch number from the mill certificate where the job requires it.
If a weld is rejected, its number leads straight to the welder, the procedure and the materials, so the cause can be found and similar welds checked.
Put a **rule or tape in the frame** so the reader can judge the size, and a **label** showing the item or weld number so the reader can find it on the job.
Take one photo to show where the defect is (the whole item) and a close-up to show the defect itself.
Keep the light even; a torch held at a low angle shows up cracks and undercut.
Log each photo as you take it: photo number, item, what it shows.
In the report, number the photos as figures (Figure 1, Figure 2), give each a **caption**, and refer to each one by its number in the text.
A simple dimensioned sketch often shows locations better than a photo. Mark a reference point and the position of each defect.

blocks.p: In a condition survey, record for every defect: the **item**, its exact **location**, what the **defect** is, its **size or extent**, the **photo number**, and how **serious** it is. A simple rating helps the reader set priorities:

head: Rating
Meaning
Example
rows: 1: Urgent
A danger to people now; make safe at once
A handrail post rusted through at its base
2: Repair soon
No immediate danger, but it will get worse
A cracked weld on a gate hinge bracket
3: Monitor
Minor; check again at the next survey
Surface rust and flaking paint on a storage rack

blocks.note: Survey from the ground or from safe access only. Do not climb on racks, rails or gates, and do not lean on or test a rail or fixing that looks damaged: report it at once and keep people away. Wear gloves when touching rusted or sharp steel. Write in the report what you could not inspect, and why.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Steel near the sea, in places such as Port Royal, Negril or Lucea, rusts much faster than steel inland, and rust hides under paint at bases, joints and anywhere water lies. Look closely at these places and record the location of each defect exactly.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The structure of a technical report

blocks.p: Most full technical reports follow the same order. Readers know where to look, and each part has its own job.

head: Part
What goes in it
Why
rows: Title page
Title, report number, issue number and date, job number, who it is for, who prepared, checked and approved it
Identifies the report and shows it was reviewed
Summary (executive summary)
In a few lines: the purpose, the main findings, conclusions and recommendations
Gives a busy reader the answer at once
Contents
Section headings and page numbers; in a long report, lists of tables and figures
Helps the reader find things
Abbreviations and glossary
Each abbreviation with its meaning; trade terms explained
Helps readers who do not know the terms
Introduction
Background and the terms of reference
Says why the report was written and what it covers
Method
What was done, how, when, with which instruments, against which standard
Lets someone else repeat the work and check the results
Findings (results)
The facts and measurements, often in tables and charts
The evidence
Discussion
What the results mean, likely causes, comparisons, any doubts
Links the evidence to the conclusions
Conclusions
What the findings show, in short statements; nothing new
Answers the question in the terms of reference
Recommendations
What should be done, by whom and by when, in order of priority
Turns the conclusions into action
References
The documents and standards used: drawings, the WPS, the code, earlier reports
Shows where each requirement came from
Appendices
Full data, record sheets, certificates, extra photos
Keeps the body short while keeping all the evidence

head: These two
The difference
rows: Findings and discussion
Findings state what was found ('undercut 0.8 mm deep at weld W7'). The discussion says what it means ('the undercut occurs on the welds made at the highest current').
Conclusion and recommendation

A conclusion says what the findings mean ('the undercut is caused by too high a current'). A recommendation says what to do ('welders to set the current within the WPS range; supervisor to check settings at the start of each shift, from Monday').
Summary and introduction
The summary gives the answer. The introduction gives the background and the terms of reference.
References and appendices
References list documents the reader can find elsewhere. Appendices are part of this report: the full data and forms.
Glossary and abbreviations list
A glossary explains words. An abbreviations list gives the full form of letters such as WPS, NDT and HAZ.

blocks.p: The summary sums up the findings, conclusions and recommendations, so it can only be written once they are finished. Keep it short (often half a page or less) and make it stand alone: a manager who reads nothing else must still know the answer and what is needed from him or her.

ul: Number the sections and sub-sections (1, 2, 2.1, 2.2) and the pages.
Number tables and figures in order (Table 1, Figure 1) and give each a title or caption.
Put long tables of readings, full record sheets and certificates in an **appendix**, and refer to them from the text: 'All 40 readings are in Appendix B.'
Do not put anything in the conclusions that the findings do not support.

blocks.p: For a small matter, use a short structure: To, From, Date and Subject; the main point in the first lines; the facts; the cause; what has been done; and what is needed from the reader. Headings still help, even on one page.

sections.title: Presenting data: tables, charts and numbers

blocks.p: Numbers are the strongest part of most technical reports, but only if the reader can see what they mean.

ul: Use a table when the reader needs the exact values, such as the leg length of each weld.
Give it a number and a title above it: 'Table 2: Fillet weld leg lengths, brackets B1 to B10'.
Put the unit in the column heading, 'Leg length (mm)', so you do not repeat it in every cell.
Keep the same number of decimal places down a column.
Show totals and, where they help, the acceptance limit beside each result, so the reader can see at once whether it passed.

head: Chart
Best for
Example
rows: Bar chart
Comparing amounts in separate groups
The number of each type of defect found this month
Line graph
Showing how something changes over time
The weekly reject rate over six months
Pie chart
Showing the parts of one whole, with only a few parts
How the month's 160 labour hours were split between four jobs
Scatter graph
Showing whether two measured values are linked
Welding current against the depth of undercut, for 30 welds
Table
Exact values, or many items
Every reading, with its limit and its result

ul: A number and a **title** that says what is shown.

Both **axes labelled with what they show and their units**: 'Current (A)', 'Undercut depth (mm)'. The **x-axis** is the horizontal axis; the **y-axis** is the vertical one. Time, or the thing you change, usually goes along the x-axis.
On a bar chart, start the vertical axis at zero: a cut-off axis makes small differences look huge.
A **key (legend)** when there is more than one set of data.
No 3-D effects or decoration that make the values hard to read.
Refer to every chart in the text and say what it shows: 'Figure 3 shows that undercut was the most common defect.'

blocks.h: Percentages: show the numbers behind them

blocks.p: A percentage on its own can mislead. '50% rejected' sounds alarming, but 1 of 2 welds is not the same as 40 of 80. Always give the count with it: **'6 of 80 welds (7.5%)'**.

An inspector checks 60 fillet welds on stair brackets and rejects 9. Some rejected welds have more than one defect. The defects found are: undercut 8, porosity 3, slag inclusions 2 and incomplete fusion 1.

head: Defect
Number found
Share of all defects
rows: Undercut
Porosity
Slag inclusions
Incomplete fusion
Total
100% (rounded figures add to 99%)

ul: The reject rate is 9 of 60 welds: 9 ÷ 60 × 100 = **15%**.
There are 14 defects in 9 welds. Say clearly whether a figure counts **welds** or **defects**, or the reader will be confused.

A **bar chart** compares the defect types. Undercut is by far the most common, so the discussion looks at its usual causes (too much current, too long an arc, travelling too fast, the wrong electrode angle), and the recommendations deal with them.
The one weld with incomplete fusion is still reported and dealt with: a rare defect can be a serious one.

blocks.note: Rounded percentages may add up to 99% or 101%. That is normal: say 'figures are rounded' under the table, rather than changing a figure to force 100%.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A spreadsheet is a good tool for any report with many readings. It can sort and filter the data; find totals, averages and the highest and lowest values (SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNTIF); work out percentages; and draw charts. Keep the raw readings on one sheet and the working on another, and check a few results by hand: one wrong cell reference can spoil every figure that follows it.

head: Write
Not
Why
rows: 6.0 mm to 6.8 mm
A clear range, the unit given, no dash that could be read as a minus sign
12 mm
12mm, 12 mms, 12 MM
A space between number and unit; unit symbols never take 's' and keep their own small or capital letters
0.8 mm
.8 mm
A zero before the point stops the point being missed
35 degrees, 120 amps, 2.5 kilos
Standard unit symbols
3 November 2026
Jamaica normally writes the day first, but American forms write the month first, so 03/11/26 can be read as 11 March; the month in words removes the doubt
Shows whether it was morning or afternoon

blocks.note: Jamaican workplaces use metric units, but you will meet inches, feet and pounds per square inch on American drawings, gauges and electrode packets. Use the units of the drawing or specification you are reporting against, and do not mix units in one table. If you convert a figure, give both: '25 mm (1 in)'.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Short sentences: one idea in each, about 15 to 20 words.
Plain words: 'use', not 'utilise'; 'about', not 'in the region of'; 'now', not 'at this point in time'.
The **active voice**, which says who did what: 'The fitter replaced the hinge pins on 4 May' is clearer than 'The hinge pins were replaced'. Use the passive only when who did it does not matter.
**One term for one thing** all through the report. If you call it a 'fillet weld' on page 2, do not call it a 'corner weld' on page 5: the reader may think it is something different.
Write each abbreviation in full the first time, with the letters in brackets, 'welding procedure specification (WPS)', and list them all near the front of a long report.
Be exact: not 'a long crack near the end', but 'a 25 mm crack at the toe of weld W4, 40 mm from the end'.
Explain any trade term the reader may not know, or put it in the glossary.

head: Type
Example
Where it goes
rows: Fact (observed or measured)
'Weld W12: undercut 0.9 mm deep over 30 mm, measured with bridge cam gauge G-02.'
Findings
Inference (a reasoned conclusion from facts)
'All the undercut is on welds made at 150 A or more, so too high a current is the likely cause.'
Discussion and conclusions, with the reasoning shown
Opinion (a personal judgement)
'The welding on this job is poor.'
Usually nowhere. If an opinion is needed, label it, give the reasons, and keep it out of the findings

blocks.p: Words like 'bad', 'terrible', 'sloppy' and 'good enough' tell the reader how you feel, not what you found. Replace each with the measurement or the limit it breaks.
A report is **objective** when it is based on facts that someone else could check, and is not swayed by personal feelings. That means:

ul: Report every result, including the unwelcome ones. Never leave out a failed test because it is awkward or because the client 'won't understand it': explain it in plain words instead.
Treat everyone the same. If a friend, a senior welder or you yourself made the faulty weld, report it exactly as you would anyone else's.
Say when something is uncertain or could not be checked: 'The inside of the tube could not be inspected.'
Do not guess at a cause and present it as fact. Say what the evidence shows and how sure you are.
Keep your original records. If you are pressed to change or remove a finding, explain politely why the facts must stay. If the pressure goes on, raise it with a more senior person.

blocks.note: Reports may be read later by clients, insurers, inspectors or a court. A false or incomplete report can put people at risk, and can make both the writer and the company liable.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A report that says only what happened ('the weld cracked') leaves the reader unable to stop it happening again. Look for why. A simple method is to keep asking **'Why?'** until you reach something the business can fix: the **root cause**.

flow: A bracket weld cracked in service. Why?
Examination showed a hydrogen crack beside the weld. Why?
The low-hydrogen electrodes used were damp. Why?
They had been left out of the rod oven overnight. Why?
No one was responsible for the oven, and the job briefing did not mention it
Root cause: no system for storing low-hydrogen electrodes; fix the system, not only the one weld

blocks.p: When you accept or reject work, say what it was judged against. 'Rejected' on its own invites argument. 'Rejected: undercut 0.9 mm deep; the WPS allows 0.5 mm (WPS-07, Rev B)' shows the limit and the document that sets it, so anyone can check the decision.
A good recommendation:

ul: follows from a finding or conclusion in the report, and deals with the cause where it can;
says exactly **what** is to be done and **where**;
names **who** should do it and **by when**;
is possible within the reader's means;
is numbered, so it can be checked off later.

blocks.p: Set recommendations out in **order of priority**: anything that affects safety first, then items that stop damage getting worse, then improvements.

head: Weak
Better
rows: Improve electrode storage.
Storeman to keep opened low-hydrogen electrodes in the rod oven and log the oven temperature each morning, starting Monday.
Fix the rails.
Contractor to cut out and replace the rusted bottom rail of the rear stair handrail, then weld, grind and prime it, within two weeks; the stair to stay closed until then.
More training is needed.
Supervisor to brief all welders on current settings for 3.2 mm electrodes at Tuesday's toolbox talk, and check settings at the start of each shift for two weeks.

blocks.h: Giving feedback on someone else's draft

blocks.p: At Level 3 you will check trainees' and colleagues' reports. Be specific and practical: point to the exact lines that are opinions or vague, show how to state the fact instead ('poor weld' becomes 'undercut 0.8 mm deep at W3'), ask for any missing evidence (units, weld numbers, photo numbers), and let the writer make the corrections so that he or she learns. Say what was done well, too.

sections.title: Special reports: incident, NCR, test, progress and survey

blocks.p: An incident investigation report records what happened, why, and what will stop it happening again. It must be accurate even in small details (times, distances, who was where), because insurers, government inspectors or a court may rely on it later.

flow: Care for anyone hurt and make the scene safe; leave it as it is where that is safe
Gather evidence early: photos, measurements, a sketch, the equipment involved, and records such as inspection tags and training records
Take short written statements from the injured person and the witnesses, one at a time, in their own words, as soon as possible
Set out the facts in time order: date, time, place, people, task, what happened, the injury or damage, the first aid given
Find the immediate cause and the root causes by asking 'why?'
Recommend actions that deal with the root causes, each with a name and a date
Have it checked, sign it, send it to the people on the circulation list, and follow up the actions

head: Cause
Meaning
Example
rows: Immediate cause
The act or condition that led directly to the harm
Spatter set fire to a welder's overalls, which were soaked with oil
Root cause
The failure in the system that allowed it
There was no check of overalls at the start of the shift, and no clean spares to change into

blocks.p: Recommendations must target the root cause. 'Tell the welder to be more careful' changes nothing; 'add clothing to the pre-start PPE check, keep clean spare overalls in the store, and have the supervisor check daily' does.

Personal details in an incident report are private. Share the report only with the people on its circulation list, and follow the company's rules and the data protection law. Lessons can still be shared with the team in a toolbox talk, without names.

Raise an NCR **as soon as** work, material or a bought-in part is found not to meet the drawing, the specification or the procedure. The sooner it is raised, the less work is built on top of the fault.

head: Part of the NCR
What it records
rows: Number, date, raised by
Identifies the NCR so it can be tracked to close-out
Job, drawing and revision, items affected
Exactly what is affected, with item numbers
Requirement
What the drawing, specification or procedure asks for, e.g. 'hole centres 150 mm ± 1 mm'
Non-conformance found
What was actually found, with measurements and photos
Containment
What was done at once: the items marked, tagged and kept apart so they are not used or sent out
Cause
Why it happened, once investigated
Disposition
The decision on the faulty items: rework, repair, use as is (with a written concession) or scrap, made by someone with the authority
Corrective action
What will stop it happening again, by whom and when
Re-inspection and close-out
The result of re-inspection, and the signature that closes the NCR

blocks.note: '**Use as is**' is not a way of hiding a fault. It needs the written agreement (a **concession**) of the person with authority, such as the client's engineer, and the NCR records it.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Identify each specimen: welder, joint, position, material and procedure.
Describe the method, or name the test procedure used, and the equipment with its calibration.
Give each result **beside its acceptance limit** from the specification, with 'pass' or 'fail'.
Attach the original record sheets, and photos of any failed specimens.

blocks.p: A progress report tells the manager whether the job is on time and on budget. Keep it short and use the same headings each week, so one week can be compared with the next:

ul: the job, the period and who wrote it;
a one-line status: on time, at risk or late, with the expected finish date;
progress against the plan: what was planned, what was done, the percentage complete;
problems, each with its **cause**, its **effect** on the finish date and cost, and the **plan** to recover;
decisions or help needed from the manager;
next period's plan.

blocks.p: A condition survey records the state of an existing item, defect by defect, so that repairs can be planned and priced. Its findings table lists each defect with its location, size, photo number and rating. Its recommendations are numbered and set out in order of priority, each with who should act and by when. It says clearly what was not inspected.

A recommendation report compares the options against the same criteria (for example cost, safety, quality, time and the skills needed), shows the comparison in a table, and ends with one clear recommendation and the reasons for it.

A completion report says what was done, the checks made and their results, any problems, and anything still open, such as a part on back order or a snag to be fixed. Listing what is still open makes sure it is followed up and the client is not let down.

ul: Every figure checked against the original record sheets; totals and percentages worked out again.
Every reading has a unit, and its decimal places match the instrument.
Weld, item and photo numbers match the sketch, the tables and the photos.
Every table, figure and appendix is numbered and referred to in the text.
The conclusions follow from the findings, and each recommendation has a who and a when.
Terms are used the same way all through; abbreviations are listed; technical terms are spelt correctly.
The summary matches the body.

blocks.p: If a draft and a record disagree (for example, the draft gives an average leg length of 6.2 mm and the spreadsheet gives 6.8 mm), do not just pick one. Go back to the original readings, find which is right, correct the error, and note what was changed.

flow: **Draft:** the first full version, written so that it can be checked
**Checked:** another competent person reviews it and signs 'checked by'
**Approved:** the person with authority, such as the manager, signs 'approved by'
**Issued:** given a report number, an issue number and a date, and sent to the distribution list
**Filed:** the signed copy and the records behind it are stored in the job file

blocks.p: The 'prepared', 'checked' and 'approved' boxes show the reader that the report was reviewed and accepted before it was issued, and who is responsible for it. The writer cannot check his or her own report: the checker must be someone else.

Once a report has gone out, never change it quietly. Make a new **issue** (Issue 2), say what changed and why in a revision table, send it to everyone who had Issue 1, and mark the old issue **superseded** so that no one works from it.

blocks.p: The **distribution list** (or circulation list) names everyone who must receive a copy. Put it on the title page or the last page, and record the date the report was sent. Send reports as a PDF where possible, so that they cannot easily be changed.

ul: Use a file name that says what the file is: the job number, the subject and the issue, for example J3108_Ramp-Frame-Inspection_Issue1.pdf. Avoid names such as 'report final new.docx'.
If you put a date in a file name, write it year-month-day (2026-11-03), so files sort in date order.
Keep the signed report and its records together in the job file, and in a backed-up folder that only the right people can open.
Keep reports for the time set by the contract, the company's rules or the law, whichever is longest. Weld records for buildings, tanks and lifting equipment may be needed for many years.

blocks.note: Power cuts, hurricanes and floods destroy paper and computers. Keep a backed-up digital copy of important reports away from the workshop, as well as the signed paper copy.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can name the main kinds of technical report and say which one suits a given question.
I can agree terms of reference: purpose, scope, reader, deadline and limits.
I can adapt the same facts for a client, a manager, a welding team and an engineer.
I can plan the data a report needs before collecting it.
I can record measurements with units, to the instrument's resolution, and correct a record properly.
I can number items and welds so each result can be traced to its welder, materials and procedure.
I can take and caption photos with a scale and a label, and refer to them by number.
I can record defects in a condition survey with location, size, photo number and rating.
I can set out a full report in the right order and say what each part is for.
I can explain the difference between findings and discussion, and between conclusions and recommendations.
I can choose a bar chart, line graph, pie chart, scatter graph or table to suit the data, and label it correctly.
I can work out percentages and always show the numbers behind them.
I can write numbers, units, ranges and dates clearly.
I can write in plain words and the active voice, keeping facts apart from opinions.
I can find a root cause by asking 'why?' and support each decision with the limit and the document that sets it.
I can write specific recommendations with who and when, in order of priority.
I can write incident, NCR, test, progress, survey and completion reports.
I can check a draft, have it checked and approved, issue it, correct it by a new issue, distribute it and file it.
I can give useful feedback on another person's draft report.

terms: A sentence in which the subject does the action: 'The welder replaced the liner'
A section at the end of a report holding full data, forms and certificates
The short description written under a photo or figure
Written agreement from the person with authority to use a faulty item as it is
A short statement of what the findings show
A report on the state of an existing item or structure, defect by defect
The list of sections and their page numbers at the front of a report
The section that explains what the results mean, before the conclusions
The decision on a non-conforming item: rework, repair, use as is or scrap
The list of people who must receive a copy of a report; also called the circulation list
The first full version of a report, written so it can be checked
A short summary at the front of a report for busy readers
The facts and measurements a report presents; also called results
A list explaining the special words and trade terms in a report
A numbered, dated version of a report that has been sent out
A report raised when work or material does not meet the requirement
Based on facts that others could check, not on personal feelings
Descriptions and observations rather than numbers
A specific action the report says should be taken, by whom and when
The list of documents and standards used in writing a report
The underlying failure in the system that allowed a problem to happen
A graph of dots for pairs of values, showing whether they are linked
Replaced by a newer issue or revision, and no longer to be used
What a report must cover, for whom, and by when
The ability to link a part to its materials, welder, procedure and inspection records
The horizontal and the vertical axes of a graph

c1.title: A cracked trailer drawbar in Santa Cruz
c1.text: Owen leads a team at a fabrication shop in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. A farmer, Mr Lindo, has brought back a cattle trailer the shop built eight months ago: the weld joining the drawbar to the 10 mm front cross-member has cracked right across. The shop owner, Ms Facey, wants a report by Friday on what failed, why, and what the shop should do about the 11 other trailers of the same design it has sold. Owen finds that the crack started along the toe, where the weld had not fused into the cross-member. The job card shows the welder used 2.5 mm electrodes at 70 A, although the WPS calls for 3.2 mm electrodes at 110–130 A. The shop has no check of welders' settings against the WPS.

c2.title: Kitchen equipment frames for a Montego Bay hotel
c2.text: Shellian is inspecting 40 welded mild steel frames that will carry cooking equipment in a hotel kitchen in Montego Bay, St James. Each frame has 4 fillet welds, so there are 160 welds in all. The drawing calls for 5 mm fillets, and the specification allows undercut no deeper than 0.5 mm. Her fillet gauge reads in 0.5 mm steps. She finds 12 welds outside the limits: 7 undersize, 4 with undercut deeper than 0.5 mm and 1 with a crack. Two welders, R and T, made the frames, and each stamped his letter beside his welds; welder R made 10 of the 12 faulty welds.

c3.title: A falling sheet of plate in Morant Bay
c3.text: At 10:40 on Tuesday morning, in the fabrication workshop of a training centre in Morant Bay, St Thomas, a sheet of 3 mm steel plate that had been leaning against a wall slid sideways and fell against a trainee, Jermaine, cutting his shin. The plate rack had been full for two weeks, so new sheets were leaned against the wall. The instructor gave first aid, and Jermaine was taken to hospital for stitches. Two trainees saw it happen. The workshop supervisor, Kerry-Ann, must investigate and write the incident report.

c4.title: Floodlight base plates for a sports ground in Falmouth
c4.text: A fabrication shop in Falmouth, Trelawny, is making 24 base plates for floodlight poles at a sports ground. The drawing, at Rev C, shows four bolt holes at 300 mm centres ± 1 mm. At the final check, Garth finds that 8 of the plates have their holes at 306 mm centres. The jig used to mark them had been set from Rev B of the drawing, which showed 306 mm. The plates are due on site in four days, and the client's engineer, Mr Wint, must approve any change to the design.

c5.title: Checking a trainee's draft in Half Way Tree
c5.text: Romario, a Level 3 trainee, has written his first inspection report, on the welded security grills fitted at an office in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. His supervisor, Ms Grant, is checking the draft. His record sheets show undercut 1.0 mm deep at weld W2 on grill 4 and porosity at weld W5 on grill 7. The draft includes these lines: (a) 'The welds on grills 4 and 7 are terrible.' (b) 'Leg lengths 5-6.5mm, cap height .8mm.' (c) The summary on page 1 was written before the inspection was finished, and does not mention the crack found later on grill 9.

questions.q: Ms Facey's request covers the cracked trailer and the 11 others the shop has sold. Which scope should go in Owen's terms of reference?
o: The whole of Mr Lindo's trailer, including its tyres, lights, floor and paint
The failed drawbar weld, its cause, and the risk to the other 11 trailers
Every trailer and gate the shop has built in the past five years
The failed weld only, since the other trailers have not come back
questions.why: The scope should match the question the reader needs answered: why this weld failed and whether the same fault may be in the trailers already sold. A wider scope wastes time; a narrower one misses the risk to other farmers.

questions.q: Which statement should Owen's report give as the root cause?
o: The weld cracked right across the drawbar joint while the trailer was being towed
The welder used electrodes that were too small, at too low a current
No one checks welders' settings against the WPS before welding starts
The farmer probably overloaded the trailer on rough country roads
questions.why: The crack is what happened, and the small electrode at low current is the immediate cause of the lack of fusion. The root cause is the missing check that let it happen, and fixing that protects every future job. The overloading idea is a guess with no evidence.

questions.q: How should the failure be reported to Mr Lindo, the farmer?
o: A copy of the full technical report, with the WPS and the settings used
A phone call only, since he has already seen the crack for himself
The same report as Ms Facey's, with all the trade terms left in
A short, plain letter: what failed, the fix, when, and a contact name
questions.why: The facts are the same for every reader, but a client needs plain words, the action and the date, and a contact. Trade terms such as WPS and toe fusion mean little to him, and a phone call alone leaves no record.

questions.q: Which photos of the crack will be most useful in the report?
o: A close-up taken from as near to the crack as the camera will focus
A close-up with a rule and a label, plus one showing its position
A wide shot of the whole trailer as it stands in the shop's yard
A close-up taken after the crack has been ground out clean and bright
questions.why: The rule lets the reader judge the size, the label ties the photo to the weld, and the wider shot shows where on the trailer it is. Grinding first destroys the evidence of how the crack started.

questions.q: How should Shellian give the reject figure in her summary?
o: 12 of 160 welds (7.5%) were outside the limits
7.5% of the welds were outside the limits
12 of 40 frames (30%) were rejected
Only a few of the welds were outside the limits
questions.why: 12 ÷ 160 × 100 = 7.5%, and giving the count with the percentage lets the reader judge it. The 12 faulty welds are not necessarily on 12 different frames, so '12 of 40 frames' is wrong, and 'a few' tells the reader nothing.

questions.q: On the record sheet, one leg length is written as 4.75 mm. What should Shellian do?
o: Leave it, since two decimal places show greater care
Round it up to 5.0 mm, since that meets the drawing
Re-measure that weld and record what the gauge shows
Change it to 4.5 mm, the nearest gauge step below
questions.why: A gauge that reads in 0.5 mm steps cannot give 4.75 mm, so the figure is a guess or a mistake. Re-measure, and record only what the instrument can show; never change a reading to suit the result.

questions.q: Welder R made 10 of the 12 faulty welds. How should this appear in the report?
o: Left out, so that R is not embarrassed in front of the client
As a fact in the findings, with a recommendation on R's settings
As a remark that R is careless and should not weld these frames
Only in a private note to R, and not in the report itself at all
questions.why: Traceability exists so that a pattern like this can be found and fixed. State it as a fact, keep personal judgements out, and recommend an action that deals with the cause, such as checking R's settings and technique.

questions.q: Shellian's first bar chart of the defects has no title, unlabelled axes, and a vertical scale that starts at 3. What must she change?
o: Add 3-D bars and a different colour for each defect type
Leave out the crack, since a single weld spoils the scale
Swap it for a pie chart, since pie charts need no axis labels
Add a title and figure number, label the axes, start at zero
questions.why: Every chart needs a number, a title and labelled axes so the reader knows what is plotted. A bar chart's axis starts at zero, or small differences look huge. The crack must stay: it is the most serious defect found.

questions.q: When should Kerry-Ann take statements from the two trainees who saw the plate fall?
o: Together, today, so that their two accounts agree with each other
At next month's safety meeting, when everyone is present
Today, one at a time, each in the witness's own words
Only if Jermaine decides to make a formal complaint
questions.why: Memories fade and get mixed with what others say, so statements are taken as soon as possible and separately. Each witness's own words are written down; the statements are not made to agree.

questions.q: Which recommendation deals with the root cause of Jermaine's injury?
o: Remind all trainees at every class to keep away from leaning plates
Put up a sign saying 'Danger: falling plates'
Jermaine to wear thicker trousers in the workshop
Add rack space, and check storage in each weekly inspection
questions.why: The plate fell because there was nowhere safe to store it and no one noticed for two weeks. More rack space removes the hazard, and the weekly check stops it building up again; signs and reminders leave the hazard in place.

questions.q: A trainee asks Kerry-Ann for a copy of the report to post in the class WhatsApp group. What should she do?
o: Agree, as long as the photos of the injury are taken out
Refuse, and share it only as the circulation list says
Agree, so that the whole class learns from the accident
Agree, once Jermaine has come back from the hospital
questions.why: An incident report holds private details and may be used by insurers or inspectors, so it goes only to the people on its circulation list. The lessons can still be shared at a toolbox talk without names.

questions.q: What should Garth do first with the 8 faulty plates?
o: Mark and tag them, and keep them apart from the good plates
Send them with the others, and note the fault on the delivery note
Re-drill the holes at once, before the delay grows any longer
Scrap them straight away and cut 8 new plates to save time
questions.why: Containment comes first: faulty items are marked, tagged and kept apart so that they cannot be sent out by mistake. Whether they are re-drilled, used or scrapped is decided afterwards by someone with authority.

questions.q: Who should decide whether the 8 plates are reworked, used as they are, or scrapped?
o: Garth, because he found the fault during the final check
The site foreman, who will set the holding-down bolts
Mr Wint, the client's engineer, who has the authority
The fitter who drilled the holes, as he knows the jig
questions.why: The disposition must be made by someone with authority over the design; here the client's engineer must approve any change. 'Use as is' would need his written concession, recorded on the NCR.

questions.q: Which entry belongs under 'corrective action' on the NCR?
o: Re-drill the 8 plates to 300 mm centres and then inspect them again
Check jig settings against the current revision; withdraw old copies
Ask Garth to check all the plates more carefully on the next job
Order 8 spare plates in case the engineer rejects the repair
questions.why: Re-drilling is the disposition: it deals with these plates. Corrective action stops the fault happening again; here the cause was a jig set from a superseded drawing, so the fix is checking against the current revision and removing old copies.

questions.q: The plates have been re-drilled. When can the NCR be closed?
o: As soon as Mr Wint agrees to the re-drilling
When the plates are delivered to the sports ground
At the month's end, along with all the other NCRs
After re-inspection, with the results recorded
questions.why: An NCR is closed only when the disposition has been carried out, the items re-inspected and found to meet the requirement, and the corrective action recorded. Agreement or delivery alone does not prove the fault was put right.

questions.q: Which is the best rewrite of line (a)?
o: Grills 4 and 7: welds of a very poor standard throughout.
Grills 4 and 7 were welded badly and need to be redone.
Grill 4, weld W2: undercut 1.0 mm deep. Grill 7, W5: porosity.
The welds on grills 4 and 7 are well below our usual standard.
questions.why: Findings give what was found, where and how big, so the reader can check and act on them. The other lines are still opinions: they say how the writer feels, not what the defect is.

questions.q: Which version of line (b) follows the rules for numbers and units?
o: Leg lengths 5.0 mm to 6.5 mm; cap height 0.8 mm.
Leg lengths 5.0mm - 6.5mm; cap height .8 mm.
Leg lengths 5 mms to 6.5 mms; cap height 0.8 MM.
Leg lengths 5mm-6.5; cap height 0.8 mm.
questions.why: Write ranges with 'to' and the same decimal places, put a space between the number and the unit, put a zero before a decimal point, and never add 's' to a unit symbol or change its letters.

questions.q: What should Romario do about the summary?
o: Rewrite it now the findings are complete, with the crack
Leave it, because the crack is already given in the findings
Move it to the back of the report, after the appendices
Delete it, because the manager will read the whole report
questions.why: A summary can only sum up the findings once they are all written, which is why it is written last. A busy reader may read nothing else, so leaving out the crack, the most serious finding, could be dangerous.

questions.q: Who should sign the 'checked by' box on Romario's report?
o: A competent person other than Romario, such as Ms Grant
The client, when the report reaches the office
Any trainee in the class who has time to read it
Romario himself, after reading it through carefully once more
questions.why: Checking means a second competent person reviews the report before it is approved and issued. A writer cannot check his own work, and the client receives the report only after it has been checked and approved.

questions.q: A supervisor wants to see whether welders who have practised more hours make fewer rejects. Which chart should the report use?
o: A pie chart of each welder's share of the rejects
A line graph of rejects for each week of the year
A scatter graph of practice hours against rejects
A bar chart of the total rejects for each month
questions.why: A scatter graph plots pairs of values, here each welder's practice hours and reject count, and shows whether they are linked. Pie, line and bar charts show shares, changes over time and comparisons, not a link between two measured values.
